hook.text: In 2014, Tesla shipped Autopilot to customers as a software update—no dealer visit needed.

buildup.text: Drivers could suddenly let the car steer itself on highways while keeping hands near the wheel.

discovery.text: Tesla used its customer fleet as a data engine—every mile driven trained its neural network.

twist.text: Critics argued Tesla was testing unfinished software on public roads with real passengers as guinea pigs.

climax.text: Fatal Autopilot crashes made global headlines and triggered federal investigations into the system.

punchline.text: Shipping early let Tesla learn fast—but at a real cost.

quiz.question: How did Tesla initially deliver Autopilot to customers?

details.summary: Tesla's Autopilot strategy deploys advanced driver assistance to millions of customer cars, using their collective driving data to train autonomous systems incrementally rather than waiting for perfection.
details.whyItMatters: Tesla's approach gathers more real-world data than any competitor but at the cost of using paying customers as test subjects on public roads, raising serious ethical and safety questions.
takeaways: Millions of Tesla cars collect driving data for AI training
The fleet-learning approach generates unmatched data volume
Multiple fatal crashes have occurred with Autopilot engaged

faq.question: How does Tesla use customer data to improve Autopilot?
faq.answer: Tesla cars run the autonomous software in shadow mode, comparing its decisions to the human driver's actions. When the AI would have made a different choice, that data is uploaded to train improved models.

faq.question: Is Tesla's approach to autonomous driving safe?
faq.answer: Critics argue it treats customers as beta testers in life-or-death situations. Tesla counters that Autopilot-engaged vehicles have fewer accidents per mile than the average human driver, though this data is debated.
